source.title: Perturbation Probing: A Two-Pass-per-Prompt Diagnostic for FFN Behavioral Circuits in Aligned LLMs
source.authors: Hong-Liang Liu; Tung-Ling Li; Yuhao Wu

page_placements.theme: Units selected for one task or concept also serve others; ablation or editing has off-target effects

record.tranche_reason: The study measures neuron overlap across distinct language-model behavioral circuits, a different measure of cross-context neuron sharing from direct activation-response analysis.
record.gate_note: The study reports a direct cross-circuit sharing result for SmolLM3-3B. Other circuit-ablation and steering results do not measure neuron polysemanticity and are not included. The text also cites findings from other work; those are not extracted as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study is about a perturbation-probing method for finding FFN behavioural circuits. Its only polysemanticity-adjacent result is Appendix M. There, 22% of top-ranked neuron slots overlap across the sycophancy, tool-use and code circuits in SmolLM3-3B. That is overlap between selected neuron sets, ranked by signed importance (output coupling times perturbation response). It is not a measure of how individual neurons respond to unrelated tokens or contexts, so no version is tested and the finding goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record paraphrases only Appendix M. The paper's main conclusion is different: perturbation probing finds causal FFN neurons only for 'opposition' circuits, where RLHF opposes pre-training (safety, sycophancy; about 50 neurons control the refusal template). 'Routing' circuits are attention-mediated and need direction injection, and the FFN/Skip ratio predicts which applies. The SmolLM3 note concludes that shared neurons are peripheral and causal neurons are circuit-specific.
record.recipe_differences: Uses perturbation probing and cross-circuit neuron overlap rather than the original sources' neuron visualization or SoLU-focused approaches.
record.method_sensitivity: not stated for the cross-circuit sharing result

fits_no_version.finding: In SmolLM3-3B, 22% of top-ranked neuron slots are shared across the sycophancy, tool-use and code-generation circuits, and 7 neurons appear in all three. Ablating all 26 shared neurons had zero behavioural effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neurons shared across behaviour-specific circuit rankings are peripheral, with weak contributions to many tasks, while causally effective neurons are circuit-specific.

record.problems: The cross-circuit sharing result is reported for one model and three circuits; uncertainty and a layer-wise breakdown are not stated for it.
record.rows_left_out: Other behavioral-circuit ablations, steering interventions, and architecture comparisons do not measure cross-context neuron sharing or another listed version of the claim.

untested.parts: No measurement of the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, nor of layer differences.
No test of superposition or capacity as the cause; the term is used loosely for circuit overlap.
Architecture comparisons concern circuit topology and FFN/Skip ratio, not polysemantic neuron share.

record.verdict_notes: The study uses 'superposition' informally for circuit-set overlap. A researcher could argue r1 weakly bears on V2, but the measure is ranking overlap among late-layer neurons in one model, with no chance baseline and no activation-level evidence of responses to unrelated inputs. The record's V2 'supports' label is therefore removed.

versions.untested_parts: Vision-model neurons and the InceptionV1 example are not tested.
The study reports circuit overlap for one model and three behavioral circuits, not a broad estimate across language models, layers, tokens, or contexts.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure or having more sparse features than neurons causes polysemanticity.
The study does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity without capacity pressure.
Architecture and training differences are discussed for behavioral-circuit topology, but their effects on the share of polysemantic neurons are not tested.
The study does not investigate whether mixed neuron responses resolve to one shared feature or related jobs.
The study does not compare activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods for classifying neurons as polysemantic.

rows.subject: SmolLM3-3B
rows.operation_detail: Measured neuron-slot sharing across sycophancy, tool-use, and code-generation circuits.
rows.value: 22% of neuron slots were shared across the circuits; seven neurons served all three simultaneously.
rows.note: The study describes this as heavy circuit superposition. It does not state a layer-by-layer breakdown or a broader prevalence estimate.
rows.check: Overlap of top-50 selected neuron sets across three circuit rankings is a selection-set statistic, not a share of neurons responding to unrelated inputs. The ranking depends on coupling to task-specific unembedding directions, which may correlate. No chance baseline, layer breakdown or exact definition of 'slots' is given.

rows.subject: SmolLM3-3B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated all 26 neurons shared across the three circuits.
rows.measure: Behavioral effect of ablating shared neurons
rows.note: The result concerns whether shared neurons causally affect the measured behaviors, rather than whether they respond to multiple contexts.
rows.check: Causal-ablation result on the shared neurons. It does not bear on whether neurons are polysemantic; correctly unlinked.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Only an appendix mentions neuron sharing across circuits. It does not test polysemanticity.

tranche.reason: The paper is a perturbation-probing method study. Appendix M is a side note on circuit-set overlap and does not test a polysemanticity version.

source_check.notes: Appendix M is four sentences with no method details: no set sizes, layers or slot-counting rule for SmolLM3-3B. Its 22% is overlap between selected circuit neuron sets that the authors call 'circuit superposition'. It is not a polysemanticity rate. Elsewhere the paper defines circuits as the top 50 neurons (Table 4, Qwen3-4B).
